reconcile.connective: Matthew Henry reads the two confessions as one testimony under different words: a witness who calls Jesus righteous has thereby affirmed what "Son of God" claims of him.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman presses the harder reading: Luke deliberately swapped Mark's "Son of God" for "innocent/righteous man" because his crucifixion scene argues legal vindication, not messianic revelation.

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.work: Jesus, Interrupted: Revealing the Hidden Contradictions in the Bible (and Why We Don't Know About Them)
skeptic.attribution: Bart D. Ehrman, Jesus, Interrupted (HarperOne, 2009), pp. 64-69

excerpts.excerpt_text: His testimony in Matthew and Mark goes further: Truly this was the Son of God. But in his case this amounts to the same; for, if he was a righteous man, he said very truly when he said that he was the Son of God; and therefore that testimony of his concerning himself must be admitted, for, if it were false, he was not a righteous man.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Henry names both Synoptic wordings explicitly and argues they amount to the same testimony — the direct harmonizing move for this exact 'Son of God' vs 'righteous man' tension.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1714)
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry treats this passage directly at Luke 23:44-49, arguing the centurion's two reported confessions 'amount to the same' testimony.

link.title: Matthew 27:54 (cf. Mark 15:39; Luke 23:47)
link.note: live apologetic treatment arguing the centurion likely said both things, with each evangelist selecting a different part
